summary:
Liberia criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. The sodomy offence carries up to one year of imprisonment, applies to women as well as men, and is a domestic-origin provision rather than a colonial import, so no external legal framework presses toward repeal.

Enforcement of the sodomy law is uncommon, but its existence deters victims of crime from reporting to police, and some people have been arrested on the basis of their sexuality or gender identity after attackers used their LGBTQ status as an excuse.

Legislative pressure on the statute is active rather than residual. Rep. Johnson N. Williams has been seeking lawmakers' support for an anti-homosexuality bill filed in the summer of 2024, and related proposals would imprison children as young as 10 years old for gay sex. Earlier rounds followed the same pattern: in 2012 new legislation proposed longer jail terms for homosexuality, and a group distributed fliers targeting gay-rights supporters.

Official hostility has been expressed at the top of the executive. In a joint interview in March 2012, then-President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf defended the laws criminalising homosexuality, remarks that drew international comment on Liberia's stance.

There is no legal gender recognition. No administrative route exists for a trans person to amend the name or gender marker on a Liberian identity document, so a visitor whose papers do not match their presentation cannot bring them into consistency before travel or during the stay.

Transition-related medical care is not available domestically. Gender-affirming hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery are not offered in Liberia, so a visitor who depends on a regular hormone supply or on post-operative follow-up has no in-country clinical fallback and must arrive with what they need.

Marriage between two people of the same sex is not recognised. In 2012 then-Senator Jewel Howard Taylor introduced a bill that would have made such a marriage a first-degree felony carrying up to ten years; it passed the Senate but not the House and never became law, and President Sirleaf had threatened to veto either of the 2012 anti-LGBTQ bills. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no recognition route.

One statutory protection sits alongside the criminal provision: Section 2.4(b)(iii) of the Decent Work Act (2015) entitles all who seek to work in Liberia to do so regardless of sex, gender identity or sexual orientation.

Community infrastructure exists but is largely private and organisational; LGBTQ Liberians often have to hide their identities in public.
tangentialFactors:
The 2012 sequence shows how external pressure has landed. Anti-gay sentiment grew after the United States announced plans to promote LGBT rights overseas, and the domestic response was new legislation proposing longer jail terms for homosexuality and fliers targeting gay-rights supporters.

The 2012 marriage bill's passage through the Senate and death in the House, together with the president's veto threat, shows the legislature and executive were not uniformly aligned on that measure. The criminal statute was untouched by either.

Statutory non-discrimination in employment and criminalisation of sexual conduct coexist in the same legal order, so a visitor's protection at work does not extend to their private life.
localsOnly:
A 2013 UN-AIDS survey put HIV/AIDS prevalence among Liberian men who have sex with men at 19.8%.

Stop AIDS in Liberia (SAIL), the first NGO founded by LGBTQ Liberians for LGBTQ people, was set up to educate men who have sex with men about HIV/AIDS, test them, and counsel those testing positive; since 2012 it has expanded its services to all LGBTQ people.

LGBTQ Liberians often have to hide their identities in public, and the private spaces where they do not are typically sponsored by SAIL or the Transgender Network of Liberia (TNOL), or created by private individuals.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the 2024 anti-homosexuality bill is unresolved in the available material: whether it has advanced, stalled or been withdrawn is not established, and no text, sponsor list or committee stage is sourced.

The scope of the proposals to imprison children as young as 10 is not detailed in the available material; the age threshold is reported but the offences and penalties attached to it are not.

A UNDP and OHCHR country report on sexual orientation and gender identity in Liberia (April 2020) is a participatory review of the legal, social and human-rights environment, but no specific finding from it is carried in the available material.

No information was identified on border or airport screening practices that would risk outing a trans traveller, nor on how Liberian identity documents record gender for the purposes of entry.

The HIV prevalence figure dates from 2013 and no more recent measurement is available in the material reviewed.
